newsitem.title: ITALY: Expect more Zaire-type crises, food summit hears.
newsitem.headline: Expect more Zaire-type crises, food summit hears.

text.p: The Zaire crisis and a global population explosion marked debate at a U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit on Thursday, with warnings of more conflict and more hunger unless the world acts to feed its people.

As the United States and other countries readied troops for a relief force in eastern Zaire, that country told the summit that the world had shut its eyes to the problem of the Hutu refugees from Rwanda and Burundi at the centre of the tragedy.

"The fate of one million human beings is being played out amid the total indifference of the international community and of the governments of the places these people are from," Deputy Prime Minister Mutombo Bakafwa Nsenda said in a speech.
He called on countries to send any aid for the refugees, who fled past ethnic slaughter, to Rwanda and Burundi to encourage their return home.
The five-day summit, hosted by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) in Rome, bringings together 194 delegations and more than 80 heads of state and government.

Security at FAO's Fascist-era headquarters was tightened on Thursday after three women stripped naked at a news conference held by U.S. Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman on Wednesday to protest against genetic manipulation of U.S. soybeans.
Most of the leaders, including veteran communist Cuban President Fidel Castro, will speak between Friday afternoon and Sunday evening when the summit ends.
It opened on Wednesday with adoption of a plan to halve the world's hungry from 840 million people in 20 years.
FAO director-general Jacques Diouf, who is from Senegal, said he welcomed moves towards international action for the refugees caught in the crossfire of fighting in eastern Zaire.
But he slammed international attitudes, saying the crisis should never have been allowed to happen.
"We should not have to wait until people are dying...to have a Robin Hood policy," Diouf told reporters late on Wednesday.
"The world is not Sherwood Forest," he said.

His call for preventive action was echoed on Thursday in the summit's debating chamber, where several speakers warned that the answer to the world's problems, including food security, lay in long-term planning and political will.
"Emergency measures alone will not rid the world of hunger," New Zealand's Agriculture Minister Lockwood Smith said.
He urged national governments to adopt policies that would bring political stability and respect fundamental rights in an effort to remove the root causes of poverty and hunger.
Another speaker, farm minister Allan Cruickshank of St Vincent and the Grenadines, told the summit: "We need to be reminded...that a hungry man is an angry man."
FAO estimates that world food production will have to increase by 75 percent over the next 30 years as the planet's population of 5.7 billion grows by a further three billion by the year 2030.

"By the middle of the next century, world population could be as low as eight billion or as high as 12 billion, a difference equal to the whole of world population in 1975," said Nafis Sadik, executve director of the U.N. Population Fund.
She urged priority action on reproductive rights, saying in a speech that again put her at odds with Pope John Paul, that action on population policy would determine food needs.
"Freedom of choice for women and men in the size and spacing of their families -- and access to the information and the means to make the choice -- remains the guiding principle," she said.
The Vatican clashed bitterly with Sadik and with the United States in 1994 over the draft platform for a U.N. population conference in Cairo which the Pope saw as encouraging abortion.
The Pontiff, a strict opponent of artificial contraception, told the food summit in an inaugural address on Wednesday, that population control was not the answer to feeding the world.

"Demography alone does not explain the inadequate distribution of food resources," he said. "It would be illusory to believe that an arbitrary stabilisation of the world population, or even its reduction, could solve the problem of hunger directly."
